review_basis: Original 2048x1152 SAP Module 02 WebP slides 09–22 visually inspected. Each scene follows displayed system flow, examples and operational constraints.
part_title: Organization Compliance, Vulnerability, Patching and Governance Review

scenes.title: AWS Config rules and conformance packs
scenes.visual_overview: Conformance-pack templates deploy related Config rules across accounts; recorders evaluate changes and optional SSM remediations require separately authorized actions.
visual_walkthrough: The top setup path deploys managed or custom Config rules and optional SSM Automation actions into selected accounts and Regions
The lower evaluation path records an S3 bucket or EBS volume change, evaluates rules, generates compliant/noncompliant findings and can start authorized remediation
An organization aggregator then provides a read-only organization view; it does not enable recorders or perform repairs.
Conclude: Conformance packs standardize rule sets; a noncompliant finding is not preventive enforcement, and remediation needs separate controls.
scenes.visual_example: The top setup path deploys managed or custom Config rules and optional SSM Automation actions into selected accounts and Regions. The lower evaluation path records an S3 bucket or EBS volume change, evaluates rules, generates compliant/noncompliant findings and can start authorized remediation. An organization aggregator then provides a read-only organization view; it does not enable recorders or perform repairs.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Conformance packs standardize rule sets; a noncompliant finding is not preventive enforcement, and remediation needs separate controls.
scenes.narration: This slide has two paths, so follow them separately. Across the top, a conformance-pack template groups AWS managed and custom Config rules with optional remediation definitions. The pack is deployed to the selected member accounts and Regions. Now look at the lower path. Each account's Config recorder tracks supported resource changes, such as an S3 bucket or EBS volume configuration. A rule evaluates the resource after a change or on its defined schedule, producing a compliant or noncompliant result. That result is a finding, not a block on the change. The next box shows optional Systems Manager Automation remediation, which needs explicitly configured permissions and approval where appropriate. Finally, an AWS Config organization aggregator collects the evaluation metadata into a centralized view across accounts and Regions. Read the yellow warnings: the aggregator does not start recording or remediate resources. For architecture decisions, conformance packs standardize detection, while proactive or preventive controls are needed to reject a violation before deployment.

scenes.title: Security Hub CSPM controls and findings
scenes.visual_overview: Accounts A, B and C contribute security posture control results to Security Hub; a public S3 bucket finding triggers triage and an explicitly executed fix.
visual_walkthrough: The three left account panels send configuration results into Security Hub
Its central dashboard highlights Account A's public-access S3 bucket
The bottom sequence enables a standard, assesses resources, creates a finding, assigns triage and verifies a changed resource
The right-hand operator corrects the bucket configuration and rechecks control compliance
GuardDuty findings refer to threat activity, not equivalent CSPM checks.
Conclude: Security Hub findings identify risk or control failures; they do not inherently prevent or automatically remediate the configuration.
scenes.visual_example: The three left account panels send configuration results into Security Hub. Its central dashboard highlights Account A's public-access S3 bucket. The bottom sequence enables a standard, assesses resources, creates a finding, assigns triage and verifies a changed resource. The right-hand operator corrects the bucket configuration and rechecks control compliance. GuardDuty findings refer to threat activity, not equivalent CSPM checks.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Security Hub findings identify risk or control failures; they do not inherently prevent or automatically remediate the configuration.
scenes.narration: This visual is about Security Hub cloud security posture management, or CSPM. On the left, three accounts represent development, test and production. Each has resources such as S3, EC2 and RDS, but the development account has a highlighted issue. Follow the arrows into Security Hub. Its central panel flags a posture finding that an S3 bucket permits public access. The right panel shows the finding's account and control context, and an operator correcting the configuration. Now read the bottom sequence. Enable the relevant security standard, assess resources, generate a finding, triage it and then recheck after remediation. That workflow requires someone or an explicitly configured automation to perform the fix; Security Hub doesn't automatically block the original misconfiguration. The slide also distinguishes this posture result from a GuardDuty finding. GuardDuty primarily detects potential malicious activity, whereas CSPM controls evaluate security configurations and compliance standards. The design lesson is to combine visibility, ownership and remediation workflows rather than treating a finding as preventive control.

scenes.title: Amazon Inspector finds vulnerabilities across accounts
scenes.visual_overview: Inspector scans supported EC2, ECR images and Lambda resources, generates vulnerability findings, and presents them centrally for prioritized fixes.
visual_walkthrough: EC2 instances, container images and Lambda code feed Inspector where supported coverage is enabled
Findings contain affected resources, severity and remediation guidance
A delegated-admin or central view gives multi-account visibility
Teams prioritize critical exposures, patch EC2 packages or rebuild vulnerable images and rescan
Inspector itself does not apply patches; coverage requirements vary by resource type.
Conclude: Use Inspector for continuous vulnerability detection and prioritize remediation, with separate patch/rebuild and validation ownership.
scenes.visual_example: EC2 instances, container images and Lambda code feed Inspector where supported coverage is enabled. Findings contain affected resources, severity and remediation guidance. A delegated-admin or central view gives multi-account visibility. Teams prioritize critical exposures, patch EC2 packages or rebuild vulnerable images and rescan. Inspector itself does not apply patches; coverage requirements vary by resource type.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use Inspector for continuous vulnerability detection and prioritize remediation, with separate patch/rebuild and validation ownership.
scenes.narration: This architecture introduces Amazon Inspector as a vulnerability detection service across AWS accounts. Begin with the three source boxes on the left: supported EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda functions. When the applicable scanning methods and coverage are enabled, Inspector analyzes these resources for relevant software or package vulnerabilities and supported code issues. Follow the arrows to the findings panel. A finding identifies the affected resource, severity and guidance for fixing the issue. A delegated administrator can view and coordinate findings centrally within configured organization coverage. On the right is the response sequence: prioritize critical issues, patch EC2 operating systems and packages or rebuild container images with corrected dependencies, then rescan to verify risk reduction. Inspector is not a patching engine, and an image finding does not automatically change a deployed container. The bottom comparison with Security Hub matters: Security Hub can aggregate Inspector findings alongside other security evidence. A robust architecture configures scanning coverage, assigns owners for remediation and confirms that the fixes actually work.

scenes.title: Systems Manager Patch Manager at scale
scenes.visual_overview: Production, development and shared-service EC2 fleets use SSM Agent, instance roles and connectivity for centrally scheduled patch baselines and compliance reporting.
visual_walkthrough: The left EC2 instances register as managed nodes with SSM Agent, appropriate IAM role permissions and HTTPS access to Systems Manager
The central patch configuration selects baselines, maintenance windows, staged deployment and compliance collection
The bottom four-step process scans, installs approved updates, reboots by policy and validates compliance and application health
An unmanaged/offline node is uncovered, not healthy
Inspector may report missing patches but doesn't apply them.
Conclude: Patch Manager coordinates controlled patch operations; always distinguish patch compliance from application health and scanning coverage.
scenes.visual_example: The left EC2 instances register as managed nodes with SSM Agent, appropriate IAM role permissions and HTTPS access to Systems Manager. The central patch configuration selects baselines, maintenance windows, staged deployment and compliance collection. The bottom four-step process scans, installs approved updates, reboots by policy and validates compliance and application health. An unmanaged/offline node is uncovered, not healthy. Inspector may report missing patches but doesn't apply them.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Patch Manager coordinates controlled patch operations; always distinguish patch compliance from application health and scanning coverage.
scenes.narration: This slide shows how to patch large EC2 fleets across production, development and shared-services accounts without treating every server as an isolated task. Start on the left. Each managed node needs SSM Agent where required, a suitable IAM instance role, and working HTTPS connectivity to Systems Manager. The central service applies patch baselines that define approved or rejected updates, maintenance windows that schedule changes, and fleet-level policy assignments. Now trace the four-step path along the bottom. Scan for missing approved patches, install them in controlled waves, reboot when the update or policy requires it, and verify both patch compliance and application health afterward. A successful patch installation alone does not prove the application is healthy. The red branch at the bottom warns about an offline or unmanaged node: without the agent, connectivity or required scope, the instance may be uncovered rather than compliant. On the right, Amazon Inspector can detect vulnerabilities or missing patches, but it doesn't actually perform the patching. Choose Patch Manager for planned, auditable change, with rollout safety and follow-up validation.

scenes.title: Govern 100 accounts without blocking teams
scenes.visual_overview: Account Factory provisions accounts with standards, Identity Center assigns teams, Organizations guardrails bound access and central security services provide evidence.
visual_walkthrough: The left self-service request enters Account Factory for a baseline account
The center Organizations hierarchy isolates security, infrastructure, production and nonproduction
Identity Center groups receive account-specific access
Right-side SCP and RCP guardrails restrict principals and resources; Config finds drift
Across the bottom CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub feed the security team
Conclude: A scalable landing zone separates centralized safeguards from delegated workload ownership and controlled exceptions.
scenes.visual_example: The left self-service request enters Account Factory for a baseline account. The center Organizations hierarchy isolates security, infrastructure, production and nonproduction. Identity Center groups receive account-specific access. Right-side SCP and RCP guardrails restrict principals and resources; Config finds drift. Across the bottom CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub feed the security team. Scoped exceptions go through review rather than bypassing inherited Denies.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A scalable landing zone separates centralized safeguards from delegated workload ownership and controlled exceptions.
scenes.narration: This scenario shows how to govern roughly one hundred AWS accounts without forcing every application change through a central operator. Start on the left with developer teams asking for a new account. Account Factory creates it with approved network, IAM, logging and tagging baselines. Follow the arrow into the AWS Organizations hierarchy in the middle. Security accounts retain log archive and audit responsibilities, infrastructure accounts own shared services, and production and nonproduction workloads receive their own boundaries. At the top, IAM Identity Center assigns developers, data, platform and security teams to particular accounts using permission sets. On the right, SCPs constrain principals and RCPs restrict supported resources; AWS Config detects deviations from the baseline. Along the bottom, organization CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub support monitoring and security investigation. An exception request is reviewed and scoped at the correct policy level, not achieved by layering a broad Allow below an explicit Deny. The key takeaway is autonomy within secure and auditable guardrails.

scenes.title: Governance architecture: who owns what?
scenes.visual_overview: AWS Organizations connects account creation, SCP/RCP ceilings, CloudTrail/Config/Security Lake evidence, security response tools and RAM infrastructure sharing.
visual_walkthrough: Four spokes surround Organizations: Control Tower and Account Factory for foundation; SCP/RCP for principal and resource limits; organization CloudTrail, Config aggregator and Security Lake for evidence; GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector and Systems Manager for detection and operational response
RAM allows eligible infrastructure sharing without transferring ownership
The bottom three teams divide platform baselines, security controls/evidence and application-level permissions and fixes.
Conclude: Separate platform governance, security operations and workload teams while preserving account isolation and centrally governed evidence.
scenes.visual_example: Four spokes surround Organizations: Control Tower and Account Factory for foundation; SCP/RCP for principal and resource limits; organization CloudTrail, Config aggregator and Security Lake for evidence; GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector and Systems Manager for detection and operational response. RAM allows eligible infrastructure sharing without transferring ownership. The bottom three teams divide platform baselines, security controls/evidence and application-level permissions and fixes.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Separate platform governance, security operations and workload teams while preserving account isolation and centrally governed evidence.
scenes.narration: This summary diagram ties together Module Two's main design responsibilities. Start in the center with AWS Organizations. The upper-left branch covers the account foundation: Control Tower and Account Factory establish managed accounts and a consistent starting baseline. On the upper right, SCP and RCP policy ceilings constrain supported principals and resources, but do not grant access. The lower-left evidence branch contains organization CloudTrail, AWS Config aggregation and Security Lake. These supply different kinds of activity, configuration and normalized security data. The lower-right branch contains GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector and Systems Manager, supporting threat detection, posture analysis, vulnerability findings and planned patch operations. Beneath Organizations is AWS RAM, which shares supported resources between accounts without transferring ownership. Now read the team responsibilities across the bottom. The platform team owns account baselines, the security team owns overarching controls and evidence, and workload teams own application permissions and fixes. The governing principle is isolated accounts, inherited controls and centralized visibility while preserving clear operational ownership.
